column1: # Constructs bash 3.2 does not have, one per row: name<TAB>regex<TAB>sample violation.
# The list is MEASURED, not remembered. Every row was run under /bin/bash (3.2.57, what
# macOS ships) and under Homebrew bash 5.3.9 and the two were compared on stdout, stderr
# and exit status; only constructs that DIVERGED are here. What bean:0049 holds is not one
# probe transcript covering this file. It is three records, and none of them covers all of
# it: evidence entry 6, a DISTILLED table of the six families that diverge silently or behind
# a diagnostic, beside one sentence recording how many of the sixteen original families
# `/bin/bash -n` rejects on its own — a table, not probe output, and not per row; the amendment
# titled "Five constructs absent from rows that already enumerate their siblings", which runs
# the eleven constructs behind the five rows added in the first review round and the
# alternatives then added to `shopt-bash4-option` and `bash4-variable`, printing each one's
# stdout, stderr and exit status under both interpreters; and the two amendments from the
# second round, "Three more rows rejecting legal bash 3.2" and "The `-v` positions are three,
# not one", which do the same for the nine lines this gate was rejecting and for
# `[ -v name ]` and `test -v name`. Amendments are named, not numbered: the ordinals move.
# The rows this file was created with therefore have no per-construct transcript anywhere:
# they were measured, and the measurement was distilled to entry 6's table rather than pasted.
# Five of them diverge SILENTLY — 3.2 exits 0, writes nothing to stderr, and produces a
# different answer. That is why this file exists at all and why running the script under a
# real 3.2 is not by itself a gate:
#   {1..9..2}      3.2 prints the literal `{1..9..2}`         5 prints `1 3 5 7 9`
#   $SRANDOM       3.2: unset                                 5: set
#   $EPOCHSECONDS  3.2: unset                                 5: set
#   $EPOCHREALTIME 3.2: unset                                 5: set
#   $BASHPID       3.2: unset                                 5: set
# and the rest exit 0 with only a line on stderr, which a script without `set -e` swallows
# — `declare: -A: invalid option` and its -g/-l/-u siblings, `mapfile: command not found`,
# `shopt: direxpand: invalid shell option name`, `printf: `a[0]': not a valid identifier`.
# `exec {fd}<f` is the one construct whose failure is loud: 3.2 exits 127. It is still here
# because 127 is a status this script never inspects either.
# The regex column is an awk ERE, matched per line against source with full-line comments
# removed. It carries no backslashes: it is used as a dynamic regex, where a backslash
# would have to be doubled and the doubling is the kind of thing that is got wrong once and
# then never looked at again.
# ANCHOR THE OPERATOR TO WHERE IT CAN OCCUR. A regex that finds the operator's characters
# anywhere on the line rejects legal bash 3.2, and a gate that rejects correct code blocks
# the next person's legitimate work. The rows that did exactly that, and a line each was
# caught rejecting. Note the second `printf-time-format` entry: the first review round
# anchored that row and shipped two fresh instances of the same defect beside the fix, which
# is why anchoring is checked against a fixture and not against the author's confidence.
#   test-v                `[[ -n "$(command -v jq)" ]]`               round 1
#   case-modification     `trimmed="${csv%,}"`                        round 1
#   printf-time-format    `printf 'coverage %d%%(min)\n' 90`          round 1
#   printf-time-format    `printf 'coverage %d%%(min)T\n' 90` and     round 2, after the
#                         `printf 'see %s\n' "use %(%Y)T for time"`   round-1 anchoring
#   brace-expansion-step  `cp {../src,../dst} .`                      round 2

# varfd-redirect `echo "{div}
"`, `sed 's/{x}
#   parameter-transform   `echo "${email:-me@u}"`                     round 2
# Each row now requires the syntax that makes the construct a bash 4 construct: `-v` in a
# test position (see below); `,`/`^` and `@X` directly after the parameter name or its
# subscript, so a `,` or an `@` inside a DEFAULT value is not one; `%(...)T` with its
# terminating `T`, introduced by a single `%` rather than the second half of a `%%`, and
# reached without crossing out of the format string; a `{n..m..s}` whose parts are integers
# or a character range, so a brace LIST holding two `..` is not one; a `{name}` redirect at a
# word boundary, so a brace-delimited placeholder inside a word is not one. Every line review
# demonstrated, and more of the same shape from the sides review did not exercise, are in the
# negative control in tools/bash-compat-lint.sh, which names them one by one — so the
# narrowing is re-proved on every run rather than trusted.
# THE `-v` POSITIONS ARE THREE ROWS, NOT ONE. `-v` is a bash 4.2 test operator wherever a
# test operator can appear: `[[ … ]]`, `[ … ]` and `test`. `test-v` covers the `[[` form and
# the `&&`/`||` that can precede it; `test-v-bracket` and `test-v-command` cover the other
# two, which nothing caught before. They are three rows rather than three alternatives of one
# because the machinery plants ONE sample per row, so three rows are three proofs and one row
# would have been one. The three regexes are mutually exclusive by construction —
# `test-v-bracket` refuses a `[` preceded by `[`, and `test-v-command` refuses a `test`
# preceded by an identifier, path or task-path character — and the planted-sample assertion
# re-checks that on every run. Measured: on `[ -v name ]` and `test -v name`, bash 3.2 writes
# `-v: unary operator expected` and the test exits 2; bash 5 exits 0 when the name is set and
# 1 when it is not, silently. Both differ from 3.2 on stderr and on status. `/bin/bash -n`
# accepts both at rc 0, so the parse half cannot reach them and this scan is the only half that
# can. The transcript is in bean:0049's amendment "The `-v` positions are three, not one".
# The sample column is not decoration. tools/bash-compat-lint.sh plants each sample into a
# fixture on every run and asserts the scan finds it, finds it EXACTLY once, and finds
# nothing in a clean fixture — the three observations doc:50-memory-and-evidence#evidence-kinds
# requires of a mechanism claiming to discriminate. A row whose sample stops matching, or
# starts matching two rules, fails the gate here rather than quietly widening or narrowing it.
# A row's ALTERNATIVES are not each planted — one sample per row is what the machinery
# checks, and these rows name substantially more constructs than there are samples. Which
# arm each row proves, and what it therefore does not, named rather than counted:
#   associative-array, declare-global, declare-lowercase, declare-uppercase
#                          prove `declare`; `nameref` proves `local`; NO row proves `typeset`
#   mapfile                proves `mapfile`, not `readarray`
#   case-modification      proves `^`, not `,`
#   parameter-transform    proves `@Q`, not `@E @P @A @K @L @U @u @a`
#   case-fallthrough       proves `;;&`, not `;&`
#   brace-expansion-step   proves the integer form, not the `{a..z..2}` character form
#   varfd-redirect         proves `{fd}<`, not `{fd}>`
#   test-v                 proves the `[[` position, not the `&&` or `||` one
#   printf-v-subscript     proves the quoted `"a[0]"`, not the bare `a[0]`
#   shopt-bash4-option     proves `globstar`, not `lastpipe inherit_errexit direxpand autocd
#                          dirspell checkjobs globasciiranges`
#   bash4-variable         proves `EPOCHSECONDS`, not `SRANDOM EPOCHREALTIME BASH_ARGV0
#                          BASHPID`
# THE CONSEQUENCE, stated because the guarantee above does not carry it: "a row whose sample
# stops matching fails the gate here rather than quietly narrowing it" holds only for the arm
# the sample exercises. A typo in any alternative named above would stop enforcing that
# construct, and the gate would stay green, because nothing plants it. Each alternative was
# run under both interpreters before being added and the transcripts are in bean:0049 — but a
# transcript records one moment, and the planted samples are what re-runs. Closing this needs
# a fourth column of extra samples, or one row per construct as the three `-v` rows now do.
# That was judged out of scope for the pull request that found it, on the ground that a
# mechanism added in a third review round is less trustworthy than a limitation stated in it.
# This is a DENYLIST and therefore fails open: a bash 4 feature nobody has named passes.
# doc:00-constitution#observed-failing says as much about enumerating shapes. It is here
# because the alternative — the interpreter — fails open on the two constructs bean:0049
# names by name, which is worse. The complementary half is the `-n` parse under the pinned
# interpreter, which does fail closed and catches every SYNTAX-level bash 4 feature,
# including ones absent from this file. Neither half subsumes the other.
# Anchoring narrows a denylist, so it trades a false positive for a miss, deliberately:
# `[[ -n "$a" ]] && [[ -v opt ]]` is caught, `[[ -v ${x} ]]` written across two lines is
# not. A miss leaves the gate where it already is on every unnamed bash 4 feature; a false
# positive stops correct work. Misses of that shape, named so they are not mistaken for
# coverage: `${arr[${a[0]}]^^}` and `${arr[${a[0]}]@Q}` are not caught, because the `[^]]*`
# spanning the subscript cannot cross the inner `]`; a `%(...)T` in a format string assembled
# from variables is not caught, because the scan sees one source line and not the value.
# WHAT IS LEFT REJECTED, AND WHY IT IS NOT ANCHORED. tools/lib/bash32-scan.awk skips
# FULL-LINE comments and nothing else, so a rule whose operator is legal inside a STRING
# LITERAL or a TRAILING comment fires on it. Two rows sit in that position and are
# deliberately left there: `pipe-both-streams` rejects `printf '%s\n' 'a|&b'` and
# `case-fallthrough` rejects `url="http://x/?a=1;&b=2"`. Both lines are legal bash 3.2 — run
# under both interpreters, byte-identical on stdout, stderr and exit status — so this gate
# WILL reject correct code of that shape, and the way past it is to move the literal out of
# the line, not to widen the scanner. They are not anchored because `|&` and `;&` outside a
# string are unambiguously the operator: there is no syntactic position to anchor to, only a
# lexical one, and a scanner that tracked quoting would be a shell lexer. Requiring trailing
# whitespace was considered and rejected — it would still reject `'a |& b'` while missing
# `run |&tee out`, buying a real miss for no real coverage. The same residue exists wherever
# an anchored rule's operator can appear inside a string: `echo "run {fd}<f"` is still
# rejected by `varfd-redirect`, because a word boundary is all there is to anchor to.
# Adding a row: run it under both interpreters first, and put a row here only if they
# disagree. A construct both accept is not a compatibility rule, it is a style preference.
associative-array
nameref
declare-global
declare-lowercase
declare-uppercase
mapfile
case-modification
parameter-transform
append-both-streams
pipe-both-streams
case-fallthrough
coproc
shopt-bash4-option
brace-expansion-step
negative-subscript
test-v
test-v-bracket
test-v-command
wait-n
printf-time-format
printf-v-subscript
varfd-redirect
bash4-variable
